meta.title: Town of Melbourne Beach — the money trail
meta.grand_total_note: Total spending across the town’s funds for the year that began October 1, 2026, as stated on the official Budget Summary the town posts (“TOTAL EXPENDITURES $5,359,912”). The Town Commission approved the budget and a tax rate of 4.6000 mills on September 16, 2026.
meta.note: Florida towns budget fund by fund for a year that runs October 1 to September 30. This is the town’s own all-funds spending total from its Budget Summary. The property tax rate stays at 4.6000 mills — 4.6% above the “rolled-back” rate of 4.3987 that would raise the same money as last year (PDF p. 23). The town also keeps $3.07 million in reserve accounts and $2.64 million in its operating account (July 31, 2026, PDF p. 22).

nodes.note: What the town expects to collect in its main fund and its building-permit fund for the year that began October 1, 2026. Property tax is budgeted at 97% of the levy, because Florida lets taxpayers pay early for a discount. These six groups add up to $5,126,817 exactly.
nodes.name: General Fund and Building Fund revenue

nodes.note: Property tax is three of every four tax dollars. The rest are taxes and fees on electric, water, gas, phone and cable bills, plus a share of gas and insurance taxes.
nodes.name: Taxes

nodes.note: Mostly building permits ($205,000), plus vacation-rental, golf-cart (LSV) and bonfire permits.
nodes.name: Licenses and permits

nodes.note: The local half-cent sales tax ($224,000), state revenue sharing ($107,271), alcohol licenses, and a $6,000 safety grant.
nodes.name: Money from the state and county

nodes.note: Almost all of it is the Brevard County School Board paying for the school resource officer ($77,000).
nodes.name: Charges for services

nodes.note: Interest on the town’s savings ($100,000) and $84,170 carried forward from last year.
nodes.name: Interest and other income

nodes.note: The levy at 4.6000 mills on $725,977,934 of taxable value is $3,339,498 (PDF p. 23). The budget counts 97% of it.
nodes.name: Property tax (4.6000 mills, budgeted at 97%)

nodes.note: The town’s main fund: police, fire, public works, town hall. The ten departments below add up to $4,704,285 exactly. The General Fund also moves $204,278 to other funds (mostly $116,250 for the town-hall bond and $74,078 for stormwater). Those dollars are counted where they are spent, in the funds below, so they are not counted twice here.
nodes.name: General Fund (001)

nodes.note: Five commissioners paid $3,000 a year each, the town clerk and deputy clerk, elections, legal notices, and records software. A $3,000 transfer to stormwater is counted in the stormwater fund.
nodes.name: Town Commission and Clerk (Legislative)
Licenses and fees (records, video, web software)

nodes.note: The town manager ($124,500, contract) and an assistant, plus $78,000 of professional services: $33,000 for grant writing and $45,000 for a non-ad valorem (special assessment) study (PDF p. 33). Honest arithmetic: the lines below, printed to the cent, add to $354,405.70; the book rounds the department to $354,406.
nodes.name: Town Manager (Executive)
Professional services — grant writing and assessment study

nodes.note: The finance manager and finance clerk, the annual audit ($35,000), a federal single audit ($3,500), and an actuarial report (PDF p. 35). Honest arithmetic: the lines add to $275,898 — $1 more than the department total the book prints. That is rounding in the town’s own book.
nodes.name: Finance

nodes.note: Up from $9,000 budgeted last year.
nodes.name: Town Planner

nodes.note: What it costs to run the town’s buildings: insurance ($151,417 across liability, flood, property, auto and cyber), phones and internet, streetlights, utilities, and $110,000 of capital — mostly a state-required elevator repair ($100,000, PDF p. 38). A $5,000 transfer to long-term capital is counted separately.
nodes.name: General Services (town hall, insurance, streetlights)

nodes.note: The Melbourne Beach Police Department: a chief, a deputy chief, two sergeants, two corporals, six officers (one is the school resource officer, paid back by the School Board) and an assistant (PDF p. 27). The largest department — 36 cents of every General Fund dollar. The police pension costs $225,481 this year. A $4,450 transfer to long-term capital is counted separately.
nodes.name: Police

nodes.note: The Melbourne Beach Volunteer Fire Department: a paid chief and three paid captains, plus about 36 volunteers who share $59,200 in stipends (PDF pp. 21, 45). Up from $401,553 two years ago, mostly because the three captain jobs are new and paid. $79,460 a year goes to Fire Engine 58, bought on a lease-purchase in FY2024 (PDF p. 80).
nodes.name: Fire
Capital — Fire Engine 58 payment and bunker gear

nodes.note: One code officer, plus a $15,000 software line. Honest arithmetic: the lines, printed to the cent, add to $90,747.95; the book rounds to $90,748.
nodes.name: Code Enforcement

nodes.note: A director, a foreman, two maintenance workers and a groundskeeper who keep up streets, parks, buildings and trees. Honest arithmetic: the lines, printed to the cent, add to $455,123.93; the book rounds to $455,124.
nodes.name: Public Works

nodes.note: Paid for by building permits, by Florida law kept apart from other town money. The building official is a contract ($120,000, “CAP Contract”). Honest arithmetic: the lines add to $218,255 — $1 over the printed total, rounding in the town’s own book.
nodes.name: Building Department Fund (125)

nodes.note: A citizen board’s small fund for environmental programs.
nodes.name: Environmental Advisory Board (104)

nodes.note: Paid for by the stormwater fee on property. Includes $72,000 of repair work (PDF p. 65). The plan sets $111,868 a year aside for emergency stormwater repairs (PDF p. 81).
nodes.name: Stormwater Utility (141)

nodes.note: No spending is planned from this savings fund this year. It holds money set aside for future equipment and buildings ($429,901, Budget Summary).
nodes.name: Long-Term Capital Projects (333)

nodes.note: The yearly payment on the 2017 Florida Municipal Loan Council bonds that refinanced the municipal complex. The 2025 audit shows $405,000 left, with the last payment on October 1, 2029 (audit p. 34). The book lists $100,000 of principal and $13,550 of interest; the other $2,700 of the $116,250 is not itemized on the page. The separate stormwater loan (Fund 202) was paid off in July 2026, so it shows $0.
nodes.name: Debt Service — Town Hall Bond (201)

nodes.note: Pipes, drains and outfalls. Last year this fund spent about $2 million of savings on projects; this year’s $77,078 comes from the General Fund. The bigger list of road and drainage projects depends on the November 3 bond vote and is not in this budget (PDF p. 81).
nodes.name: Stormwater Projects (341)

nodes.note: Paid from savings set aside in this fund. The yearly “pave and mill one mile” line was removed “in lieu of GO Bond” (PDF p. 80).
nodes.name: Road Paving and Repairs (351)
Historic buildings — Ryckman House and Old Town Hall (390, 391)

nodes.note: Parking meters at Ocean Avenue Park and Ryckman Park are budgeted to bring in about $240,000 this year ($140,500 and $99,900). That money pays for lifeguards ($24,202), park upkeep, town events, playground and court repairs ($30,000) and transfers to other funds (PDF pp. 66–71). These two funds are in the budget book but not in the official one-page Budget Summary total — Docket #2.
nodes.name: Beach parking funds (172, 175)

nodes.note: Small funds from donations and fees: fire donations ($18,000 planned spending), police education ($1,500), police donations ($2,150). Fund 122 held $167,510 that the town received for police work for another government (“Police Services to Other Governments”) and the book shows $154,593 spent from it (PDF pp. 25, 58).
nodes.name: Police and fire donation funds (103, 121, 122, 622)

nodes.note: The county is a separate government with its own budget. On a Melbourne Beach tax bill (millage code 34X0) it levies 2.8643 mills for its general fund, plus the library district (0.3242), mosquito control (0.1340), South Brevard Recreation District (0.3000) and environmentally endangered lands (0.0733). The Brevard County Sheriff runs the county jail. The county budget is not ingested yet — Docket #3.
nodes.name: Brevard County

nodes.note: The largest piece of most tax bills: 6.3100 mills in 2025 — 3.0620 set by state law, 0.7480 by the local board, 1.5000 for buildings, and 1.0000 that voters approved for teacher pay. Not ingested yet.
nodes.name: Brevard Public Schools
